subject: Agriculture
title: CRISPR in Agriculture
description: A 60-second lesson on CRISPR in Agriculture.

hook.text: CRISPR can edit a single letter of DNA in a crop's genome—faster, cheaper, and more precise than any tool before.

buildup.text: Traditional breeding takes 10–15 years to develop a new variety. CRISPR can achieve changes in months.

discovery.text: CRISPR-edited crops include non-browning mushrooms, drought-tolerant corn, and higher-yield tomatoes.

twist.text: Some countries regulate CRISPR like GMOs. Others treat it like conventional breeding. There's no global consensus.

climax.text: If CRISPR crops are deregulated, smallholder farmers could access improved varieties without corporate patents.

punchline.text: A bacterial defense system became agriculture's sharpest tool.

quiz.question: What makes CRISPR different from traditional plant breeding?
options: It precisely edits specific DNA letters in months instead of years

details.summary: CRISPR in agriculture applies gene-editing technology to make precise, targeted changes in crop and livestock DNA. This topic covers how CRISPR accelerates development of disease-resistant, climate-adapted, and more nutritious food plants and animals.
details.whyItMatters: Climate change is outpacing traditional breeding timelines. CRISPR can deliver new crop traits in a fraction of the time, helping agriculture adapt to rapidly shifting conditions.
takeaways: CRISPR can create beneficial mutations identical to those found in nature
Gene-edited crops are reaching farmers faster due to lighter regulatory pathways
CRISPR livestock applications include disease-resistant pigs and hornless dairy cattle

faq.question: How does CRISPR differ from traditional GMO technology?
faq.answer: Traditional GMOs insert genes from other species into a plant. CRISPR makes targeted edits to the plant's own existing DNA, mimicking mutations that could occur naturally through breeding, just far more quickly and precisely.

faq.question: What CRISPR-edited crops are already available?
faq.answer: Japan has approved CRISPR tomatoes with higher GABA content. The US has cleared CRISPR-edited soybeans with healthier oil profiles and browning-resistant mushrooms. Disease-resistant wheat and rice are in advanced trials.
